name: Cetylpyridinium chloride mouthwash

lead: CPC mouthwash is the common over-the-counter antibacterial rinse, sold for plaque, gum inflammation and bad breath. People use it for a fresher mouth and cleaner-feeling teeth between brushings.

CPC is a positively charged quaternary ammonium compound that binds to and disrupts bacterial membranes. Reviews report a small added benefit over brushing alone for plaque and gum inflammation, generally less than chlorhexidine. During COVID-19 it also drew research interest because it disrupts the membranes of some viruses.

paras: It is a standard drugstore rinse used after brushing, often daily, usually as part of a routine with floss or interdental cleaning. Results on breath are felt quickly, while plaque effects build with regular use.
Tooth staining is reported in roughly 3 percent of users, and taste changes are usually temporary. The US FDA monograph covers short-term over-the-counter use.

angle.text: CPC rinses cut mouth bacteria, plaque and bad breath, which helps give you a fresher mouth and cleaner-looking teeth and gums. Studies show a modest added plaque benefit that is weaker than chlorhexidine, with some staining reported.

lead: Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) mouthwash is an over-the-counter antiseptic rinse built around a quaternary ammonium compound that kills bacteria and disrupts the membranes of enveloped viruses.[1] Typical products contain about 0.05 percent CPC and are sold for plaque, gingivitis and bad breath.[2] The appearance payoff is a cleaner mouth: less plaque on the teeth, calmer and less inflamed gums, and fresher breath, which affect how a smile and close-up presence come across.[2][3][1]

Reviews report a small but significant added benefit on plaque and gingivitis when CPC rinses are used with toothbrushing, generally less than chlorhexidine.[1][4] Tooth staining and temporary taste changes are reported side effects.[1] During the COVID-19 pandemic, CPC rinses were also trialled for reducing SARS-CoV-2 in saliva.[5][6]

CPC is a long-standing ingredient in drugstore rinses such as Crest Pro-Health, launched in April 2005, and in lozenges, toothpastes and breath sprays; Wikipedia counted over 125 over-the-counter oral care products containing it as of September 2012.[1]
infobox: Oral rinse, also lozenges, sprays and toothpastes[1]
0.025 to 0.1 percent, labeled for short-term OTC use[1]

paras: CPC is used in mouthwashes, toothpastes, lozenges and throat sprays.[1] Randomised trials have compared 0.05 percent CPC rinse with 0.12 percent chlorhexidine for plaque and gingival inflammation, and with tea tree oil rinses in a short plaque regrowth model.[7][2] A 2025 double-blind trial examined CPC rinse on halitosis and tongue microbiota in people in orthodontic treatment.[3]

With chlorhexidine and zinc lactate, CPC has been found effective against halitosis, according to Wikipedia.[1] A 12-week randomized trial of a regimen combining stannous fluoride toothpaste, a rinse with 0.075 percent CPC and 0.28 percent zinc lactate, and a foaming toothbrush reported significant plaque and gingivitis reductions versus a non-antibacterial regimen from week 1 onward.[8]

Wikipedia and its cited reviews describe CPC as adding a small benefit to brushing for plaque and gingivitis.[1] A 1997 six-week double-blind study of 129 people examined effects on normal oral flora and on colonisation by non-oral species.[9] An in vitro study compared 0.05 percent chlorhexidine and 0.05 percent CPC against bacteria in biofilms, and another trial examined rinses before dental implant surgery and toothbrush disinfection.[10][11][12]

In a double-blind trial in 219 university students, alcohol-free 0.05 percent CPC and 0.12 percent chlorhexidine rinses each reduced plaque and gingivitis compared with placebo after six weeks, with no significant difference between CPC and chlorhexidine; staining scores were lower with CPC than with chlorhexidine, though not significantly so.[2] A randomized crossover trial examined CPC rinse on denture plaque and the oral microbiome.[13]

Wikipedia reports tooth staining in about 3 percent of users, and a small percentage notice temporary taste alteration that resolves a few days after stopping. Concentrated solutions irritate mucous membranes.[1] The manufacturer of Crest Pro-Health has said staining reflects the product working, because dead germs can collect on teeth, and a small back-label warning about surface staining is carried on the product.[1]

Procter and Gamble faced a class action filed in August 2009 over staining from a CPC rinse, which a US District Court dismissed in July 2010.[1] An in vitro study (2017) reported mitochondrial interference at concentrations that the authors said may be relevant to human exposure.[1] The FDA monograph concluded that 0.025 to 0.1 percent CPC is safe as an over-the-counter oral antiseptic when labeled for short-term use of up to seven days.[1]

A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in 118 SARS-CoV-2 positive outpatients compared 1-minute rinses with 0.07 percent CPC or coloured water; viral RNA load in saliva did not differ significantly between groups, while nucleocapsid protein from lysed viruses was higher in the CPC group at 1 hour.[5] A 2023 systematic review of randomized trials reviewed efficacy against the virus, and a lipidomics study found oral rinses disrupt the viral envelope in vivo.[6][14]

Plaque and gingivitis trials versus chlorhexidine and tea tree oil are described above.[7][2] A 1997 six-week double-blind study of 129 people examined effects of 0.05 percent CPC used twice daily on normal oral flora and on colonisation by non-oral species.[9] A 2025 double-blind trial examined CPC rinse on halitosis and tongue microbiota in people in orthodontic treatment.[3] Other trials examined rinses before dental implant surgery and toothbrush disinfection.[11][12]

timeline.event: A CPC-based rinse launches in the US market.[1]
Six-week double-blind study of 0.05% CPC rinse on normal oral flora published.[9]
Class-action suit over tooth staining filed; dismissed in 2010.[1]
Randomised trial of CPC rinses on SARS-CoV-2 shedding published.[5]
